la:other:Galli.html:
Galli, ōrum, m.,
the Gallic nation, the Gauls, both beyond the Rhine and in Upper Italy; afterwards also in Phrygia as Gallograeci or Galatae.—Of the Gallograeci, —In sing.: Gallus, a Gaul: delegit Gallum ex his, quos auxilii causa secum habebat,; cf.: Gallus inter Gallos sine ulla suspicione versatus,.—In fem.: Galla, ae, a female Gaul: inter quae (sacrificia extraordinaria) Gallus et Galla, Graecus et Graeca in foro boario sub terra vivi demissi sunt,.—Hence the pun with galla, gall-nut, .—
Derivv.
Gallĭa, ae, f., the country of the Gauls, Gaul, both beyond the Rhine and in Upper Italy; the more precise name of the former is Gallia ulterior or Transalpina, and of the latter Gallia citerior or Cisalpina, v. h. vv.—Hence, in plur.: Galliae duae (provinciae) quas hoc tempore uno imperio videmus esse conjunctas,.—
Gallĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Gauls, Gallic: muli viliores Gallicis cantheriis,: ager,; : humus,: Oceanus,; cf. sinus,: arma,: naves,; 3, 14, 7: bella,: lingua,: mores,; cf. consuetudo,; 5, 14, 1: ostentatio, al.: canis,a greyhound,: ventus,the north-northeast wind,. —Subst.: gallĭca, ae, f., a Gallic shoe: (redii) cum calceis et toga, nullis nec gallicis, nec lacerna,; cf. .—Adv.: Gallĭce, in Gallic: a Gallo et a Mauro Gallice et Maurice dicimus,

Varr. ap. ; .— *

Gallĭus, a, um, adj., Gallic: Galliae pro Gallicae, lib. IV.: duae Galliae mulieres conventum vitantes, etc.,—
Gallus, a, um, adj., Gallic: Galla credulitas,: mulieres, Dietsch.—
Gallĭcānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Roman province Gallia (in Upper Italy), Gallican: legiones,: ratio atque res,: ager, (al. Gallicus, like ib. § 6): lana, Müll.—Also in gen. for Gallic: catulus,: jumenta,.—Subst.: Gallĭcāni, ōrum, the Gallicans, .—In sing.: m., the inhabitants of the province Gallia, prius enim Gallus, dein Gallicanus, extremo Semiplacentinus haberi coeptus est, init.—*
Gallŭlus, a, um, adj., Gallic: Roma, poet. of the city Arelas, in southern Gaul, .

senses: to rejoice, make merry
to take pleasure in, be pleased with, delight in, enjoy
la:verb:gaudeo.html:
gaudĕo, gāvīsus, 2 (archaic
perf. gavisi, Liv. Andron. and Cass. Hem. ap. P.), v. n. and a. [Gr. γαίω, rejoice, for γαϝιω; cf. gavisus; root γαυ-; γηθέω, γάνυμαι, etc.; cf. ἀγαυρός, proud, ἄγη, astonishment], to rejoice, be glad or joyful respecting any thing, to take pleasure in, be pleased with, delight in (of inward joy, opp. laetari, to show one's self glad, exhibit joy; cf.: gaudere decet, laetari non decet, quoniam docendi causa a gaudio laetitiam distinguimus,); usually constr. with an object-clause, quod, the abl., or absol.; less freq. with the acc., cum, quia, the gen., si, etc.
With acc. and inf. or the simple inf.: quae perfecta esse gaudeo vehementerque laetor,; cf.: quem tamen esse natum et nos gaudemus et haec civitas dum erit laetabitur,: salvum te advenire gaudeo,: venire tu me gaudes?: quos sibi Caesar oblatos gavisus,: animus aliquid magnum agere gaudet,; ; : laudari in bonis gaudent,: in domo vires remansuras esse gaudebant,; Sen. ap. : iterare culpam,; ; cf.: motus doceri gaudet Ionicos,; : laedere gaudes,: spargere gaudes argumenta viri,.—
With quod: sane gaudeo, quod te interpellavi,: gaude, quod spectant oculi te mille loquentem,: quod scribis te a Caesare cottidie plus diligi, immortaliter gaudeo,; cf.: bonis viris quod ais probari quae adhuc fecerimus, valde gaudeo,.—
With abl.: ipsa liberatione et vacuitate omnis molestiae gaudemus, omne autem id, quo gaudemus, voluptas est,: correctione,: illis,: aequitate justitiaque,: hoc scientiae genere,: praeda ac populationibus, magis quam otio aut requie,: scaena gaudens miraculis,: equis,: equis canibusque,: rure,

: pictis tabellis,: carmine (with delectari iambis),: gaude sorte tua,; cf.: ille cubans gaudet mutata sorte,: ero gaude,i. e. at your master's return,; ; ; ; 7, 105.—Prov.: gaudet patientia duris,.—

Absol.: tristis sit (servus), si eri sint tristes: hilarus sit, si gaudeant,; : gaudebat, me laudabat,: gaudeat an doleat,: et irasci nos et gaudere fingimus,: si est nunc ullus gaudendi locus,: de Bursa, te gaudere certo scio,: admonebo, ut in sinu gaudeant, gloriose loqui desinant,.— (ε) With acc. (usually with homogeneous or general objects): hunc scio mea solide gavisurum gaudia,; cf.: ut suum gaudium gauderemus, Cael. ap. ; : jam id gaudeo,; cf.: gaudeo, etsi nil scio quod gaudeam,: hoc aliud est, quod gaudeamus,; : quod gaudere posset, hoc fuit,: nunc furit tam gavisos homines suum dolorem, Cael. ap. : gaudent natorum fata parentes,: tu dulces lituos ululataque proelia gaudes,.—In pass.: ista pars gaudenda mihi potius quam, etc.,.—(ζ) With cum, quia, si, in, etc.: quom gravidam et quom te pulcre plenam aspicio, gaudeo,; ; : quom tu's liber, gaudeo,: quia vos tranquillos video, gaudeo et volupe est mihi,: Er. Gaude. He. Quid ego gaudeam? Er. Quia ego impero. Age, gaude modo, : gaudes, si cameram percusti forte,: mea Clotho et Lachesis gaudent, si pascitur inguine venter,: crudeles gaudent in tristi funere fratris,: in puero, (28): tibi gratulor, mihi gaudeo, te amo,I for my part, as for myself,; v.in the foll. the passage .—
Like χαίρειν of inanim. and abstr. things, to rejoice in, delight in any thing (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose): nec tantum Phoebo gaudet Parnasia rupes,; : postquam oleo gavisa cutis,: umore omnia hortensia gaudent,: rastris atque ablaqueationibus (myrrha), § 66: addebantur et laudes, quibus haud minus quam praemio gaudent militum animi,: oratio gaudebit occasione laetius decurrendi,: (paeon) ante se brevibus gaudet pyrrhichio vel choreo,; : (vites) Amineae pingui arvo maxime gaudeant,: id (sc. consilium, animus) sibi solum per se sapit: id sibi gaudet,rejoices for itself,.—
In partic.
In sinu or in se, to rejoice within one's self or secretly, to feel a quiet joy: ut in sinu gaudeant,: qui sapit, in tacito gaudeat ille sinu, (cf.: in tacito cohibe gaudia clausa sinu, (3, 20), 30): tam gaudet in se tamque se ipse miratur,.—
Like the Gr. χαίρειν, as a word of salutation (pure Lat. salvere): Celso gaudere et bene rem gerere Albinovano Musa rogata refer,take my greetings to Celsus,; so .—Hence, gaudens, entis, P. a., joyful, cheerful (very rare): interea cum Musis nos delectabimus animo aequo, immo vero etiam gaudenti ac libenti,; (4, 13), 9; : si quis Forte coheredum senior male tussiet, huic tu Dic ... gaudentem nummo te addicere,with pleasure, gladly,.—Adv.: gauden-ter, rejoicingly (late Lat. and rare), Pseud.

la:noun:gaudium.html:
gaudĭum, ii (apoc. form gau, like cael for caelum, do for domum: replet te laetificum gau, Enn. ap. Auson. Technop. 144; Ann. 451 Vahl.), n.
id.
,
inward joy, joy, gladness, delight (opp. laetitia, joy which shows itself externally).
Lit.
In gen.
Sing.: cum ratione animus movetur placide atque constanter, tum illud gaudium dicitur: cum autem inaniter et effuse animus exsultat, tum illa laetitia gestiens vel nimia dici potest, quam ita definiunt sine ratione animi elationem,; : voluptas dicitur etiam in animo ... non dicitur laetitia nec gaudium in corpore, (cf. under B.): veluti ex servitute erepta (plebs) gaudium atque laetitiam agitabat,: exsultare laetitia, triumphare gaudio,: meum factum probari abs te triumpho gaudio, Caes. ap. , A, 2: non possum non confiteri, cumulari me maximo gaudio, quod, etc.,: gaudio compleri, gaudio afficere,: tuis litteris perlectis exsilui gaudio,; cf.: cum tuas litteras legissem, incredibili gaudio sum elatus,; : gaudium, tristitiam ostendimus (manibus),: missa legatio quae gaudio fungeretur,to express their joy, offer their congratulations,: prae gaudio ubi sim nescio,; cf.: nimio gaudio paene desipere,: exclamare gaudio,; cf.: lacrimare gaudio,: Ha. Gaudio ero vobis. Ad. At edepol nos voluptati tibi, : quid illud gaudii est?.—With an object-genitive: gaudium periculosi saltus superati,.—
Plur.: quocum multa volup ac gaudia clamque palamque, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 247 Vahl.): cum me tantis affecistis gaudiis,; more freq., the outward expressions of joy: feminarum praecipue et gaudia insignia erant et luctus, (cf. sing.: gaudio exultans,): quibus gaudiis exsultabis?: ita varie per omnem exercitum laetitia, maeror, luctus atque gaudia agitabantur,: o qui complexus et gaudia quanta fuerunt!: gaudia prodentem vultum celare,: in tacito cohibe gaudia clausa sinu, (3, 20), 30 (cf. gaudeo, II. A.): hunc scio mea solide gavisurum gaudia,: scin' me in quibus sim gaudiis?.—Prov.: Gaudia principium nostri sunt doloris,.—
In partic., sensual pleasure, delight, enjoyment (rare; not in Cic.; cf. above the passage,; usually in plur.): dediti corporis gaudiis per luxum et ignaviam aetatem agunt,: mutua gaudia,; : communia,; cf. ; ; : non umquam reputant quanti sibi gaudia constent,: vini atque cibi,: cenae,.—In sing.: mihi sibique pestiferum hinc abstulit gaudium,.—
Transf., also, like our joy, for an object which produces joy, a cause or occasion of joy (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose): ceterum hoc gaudium magna prope clade in Samnio foedatum est,: non animo solum patrio gratum munus, sed corpori quoque salubre gaudium (sc. reditus filii) fuit,: cupidus falsis attingere gaudia palmis, i. e. conjugem,: fugiunt tua gaudia,; ; .—
Of inanim. and abstr. things: non omnes (arbores) florent, et sunt tristes quaedam, quaeque non sentiant gaudia annorum,: flos est gaudium arborum,: adamas opum gaudium, § 2.

Gāĭus (less correctly Cāĭus;
trisyl.,; ; ); gen. Gāi (voc. Gāi, ), m., and Gāĭa, ae, f.
for Gavius; from gaudeo
, a Roman prœnomen, usu. written C.; v. the letter G. Gaia was written O, ; Vel. Long. p. 2218; P. prol. p. 1502.— At marriage festivals it was customary to call the bridegroom and bride Gaius and Gaia, Fest. s. v. Gaia, p. 71; Quint. l. l.; —
In partic.
An eminent jurist who lived about A.D. 110-180, author of the Institutionum Commentarii IV., which contain a systematic summary of the Roman law of family relations, of private property, and of actions; and which for generations was a standard educational work on the subject. This work was known, however, to modern scholars only by the fragments preserved in the Pandects, etc., until in 1816 Niebuhr discovered in the Chapter House of Verona a nearly complete MS. of the original work of Gaius, over which works of St. Jerome had been written. Teuffel, Gesch. d. Röm. Lit. p. 812 sqq.—
In post-Aug. historians, esp., the emperor Gaius Caligula; hence, Gāiānus or Cāiānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Caligula: custodia,: clades,fin.: expeditiones,: nex,: as (because lowered in value by him),.

la:noun:Gaius.html:
Gāĭus (less correctly Cāĭus;
trisyl.,; ; ); gen. Gāi (voc. Gāi, ), m., and Gāĭa, ae, f.
for Gavius; from gaudeo
, a Roman prœnomen, usu. written C.; v. the letter G. Gaia was written O, ; Vel. Long. p. 2218; P. prol. p. 1502.— At marriage festivals it was customary to call the bridegroom and bride Gaius and Gaia, Fest. s. v. Gaia, p. 71; Quint. l. l.; —
In partic.
An eminent jurist who lived about A.D. 110-180, author of the Institutionum Commentarii IV., which contain a systematic summary of the Roman law of family relations, of private property, and of actions; and which for generations was a standard educational work on the subject. This work was known, however, to modern scholars only by the fragments preserved in the Pandects, etc., until in 1816 Niebuhr discovered in the Chapter House of Verona a nearly complete MS. of the original work of Gaius, over which works of St. Jerome had been written. Teuffel, Gesch. d. Röm. Lit. p. 812 sqq.—
In post-Aug. historians, esp., the emperor Gaius Caligula; hence, Gāiānus or Cāiānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Caligula: custodia,: clades,fin.: expeditiones,: nex,: as (because lowered in value by him),.
